channel.title: EverythingTech
channel.description: A daily tech newspaper. 47 sources, read in full and edited by an LLM every morning.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5 debuts at 75% lower cost than its predecessor
item.description:
Anthropic's smallest model now runs cheap and fast enough to replace older systems, with an adjustable reasoning dial to trade speed for accuracy.

Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5, a major update to its lightweight model for high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads. The new version costs around 75% less than Haiku 4.5, making it competitive for summary generation, database queries, and classification tasks. It's also Anthropic's fastest model to date, well-suited for real-time interactions like customer support.

The headline feature is an adjustable reasoning dial, letting builders trade inference speed against answer quality—brand new to the Haiku line. Alignment and safety guardrails got stronger across the board. Nine out of ten Haiku requests use prompts shorter than 100,000 tokens, which means the 75% price drop directly unlocks new feasible architectures: edge AI and enterprise-scale categorization where per-token costs were prohibitive before.

Anthropic also cut cache-read pricing for Sonnet 5.5 and introduced monthly API spending allowances for Max and Team plan members.

item.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft unveil RTX Spark, positioning local AI agents as a Windows first-class feature
item.description:
The two companies are embedding AI agent execution directly into Windows as a platform primitive, not a bolted-on application.

At a Microsoft event in San Francisco, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined how RTX Spark—NVIDIA's first Arm-based PC chip—and new Windows infrastructure will make AI agents native to the operating system. The announcement positioned personal computers not just as tools for running agents, but as the runtime environment where agents live.

Microsoft announced Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), a platform layer for running agents persistently and safely in the background with OS visibility and governance. Nadella's pitch centered on security: making Windows a fortified environment for agents. Huang traced NVIDIA's 30-year Windows alliance to position agents as a natural next step, not an afterthought. The target isn't server rooms but personal computers themselves: machines where agents live as first-class OS citizens, alongside the security and telemetry that implies.

item.title: GPT-6 gets interactive visuals built into ChatGPT's responses
item.description:
OpenAI trained GPT-6 to generate diagrams, charts, buttons, and interactive forms inline with text, turning responses into lightweight applications.

OpenAI rolled out Intelligent UI, a new feature in ChatGPT where GPT-6 can respond not just with text but with interactive visuals: diagrams, charts, tappable buttons, forms, and even small tools. The model was trained to decide when visuals add value over text and how to format them correctly. OpenAI showed examples of ChatGPT generating a labeled diagram of a bicycle when asked about design, or teaching Mahjong by rendering clickable tiles and categories.

The change applies to all ChatGPT tiers—Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users get it immediately, with free and Go tiers following shortly. Higher tiers get GPT-6 Sol; free and Go users get Luna. The update also improves ChatGPT's web search and partial-response streaming while GPT-6 gathers more information. OpenAI reports stronger resistance to safety-training bypasses in GPT-6 compared to earlier models.

item.title: Sharing AI progress in mathematics
item.description:
OpenAI released findings on 377 math problems solved by internal models, fueling debate about whether AI reasoning or pattern completion is the actual bottleneck.

OpenAI shared research results on 377 mathematics problems spanning algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic, and topology, solved by internal models not yet released publicly. The release sparked discussion in the field about whether OpenAI's systems achieved creative mathematical reasoning or simply completed final steps of proofs after absorbing human mathematicians' ideas. OpenAI provided detailed writeups on 10 of the solutions to show how models arrived at answers.

The announcement matters less for any single result than for the signal: frontier models are now tested on open-ended mathematical problems, not closed benchmarks, and the field is grappling with how to evaluate whether the thinking is genuinely novel.

item.title: Microsoft launches Surface Laptop Ultra starting at $2,599, powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark
item.description:
Microsoft's flagship laptop bets the developer market on NVIDIA's new Arm-based chip, undercutting MacBook Pro prices while bundling Windows AI infrastructure.

Microsoft released pricing and details for the Surface Laptop Ultra, its new laptop powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark Arm chip. The base model starts at $2,599 with an 8-core CPU, 24GB RAM, and 512GB storage, shipping October 16. The machine switches from Microsoft's proprietary Surface charging to USB-C and leverages RTX Spark's unified memory to give developers choice between local AI tasks and traditional workloads—The Verge reported that even AAA gaming titles run smoothly on the hardware.

Also announced: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a $5,999 mini PC for developers arriving in November, with 128GB unified memory and one petaflop of AI compute performance. Both products tie directly into Windows AI updates, including Hybrid Intelligence, which lets Copilot access local files and take OS-level actions. Microsoft is positioning this hardware as the foundation for its "agents on Windows" strategy.

item.title: Stack Overflow survey finds 80% of developers using AI daily, but morale is slipping
item.description:
Developers trust AI tools more than ever (87% have some level of confidence in AI outputs, up from 31% last year), yet report lower job satisfaction and burnout.

Stack Overflow surveyed over 30,000 technologists from 169 countries on their work, happiness, and AI adoption. The headline: developers are using AI at unprecedented levels (80% report at least an hour of daily AI use), and trust in AI outputs surged from 31% to 87% in a single year. But overall job satisfaction declined compared to the prior year. Stack Overflow CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar attributed the paradox to a fundamental role shift: "With AI, every individual becomes almost a manager of agents." Agents are multiplying some developers' output, but the transition strains those who haven't adapted.

The survey reinforces what other researchers are finding: the productivity gains are real, but uneven. Those leveraging agents effectively report superpowered workflows; those caught between old and new practices report friction.

item.title: "Software is over": Open-source developer uses Claude to build clean-room Adobe alternatives in Rust
item.description:
One developer published Rust reimplementations of Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and other Adobe tools, using Claude Opus 5.5 for reverse engineering, vowing 99% feature parity in months.

A software developer named Brandon Thomas announced Artcraft, a suite of seven open-source applications built in Rust that replicate the user interface and core functionality of Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Thomas used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 to accelerate the "clean-room" implementation—building from first principles, not copying Adobe's code. WebAssembly versions let users run the tools in a browser.

Thomas promised rapid progress, initially claiming full parity within a month, then retreating to a more measured "99% in months, not years." The work is in super-early alpha, with commenters on Hacker News pointing out significant shortcomings. But the announcement signals the plausibility of AI-accelerated reverse engineering for widely-used interfaces and a willingness in the open-source community to tackle expensive, closed software.

item.title: OpenAI releases detailed findings on 377 math problems
item.description:
OpenAI published solutions to mathematics problems spanning multiple domains, opening debate on whether frontier models are reasoning or pattern-completing off human work.

OpenAI published research showing 377 mathematics problems solved by internal models across algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic, and topology. The company provided detailed explanations for 10 solutions to demonstrate the reasoning path. The release sparked immediate debate in the mathematics and AI communities about whether models achieved genuine creative reasoning or completed final steps by absorbing and synthesizing human mathematicians' work. The models used remain unreleased and may not be publicly available soon.

The significance lies less in any single result and more in the signal: frontier models are now evaluated on open-ended mathematical problems where the boundary between reasoning and pattern completion matters.

item.title: Mistral launches "Le Chonk," a 1-trillion-parameter open-weight model to compete with frontier labs
item.description:
Mistral published Le Chonk: a trillion-parameter model you can download and run, trained in Paris, built for developers and defensive security teams.

Mistral released a public preview of Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with 52 billion active parameters. The company trained it from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European datacenters, a significant infrastructure milestone. Le Chonk targets coding, agentic workflows, and cybersecurity, with state-of-the-art performance in regulated domains like finance and law.

The model prioritizes organizational control and autonomy: it's open-weight, available across multiple regions including a European deployment under European law, and paired with reduced moderation to enable legitimate security research and incident response. Full weights drop at month's end; Mistral is currently red-teaming with security teams and vetted partners. On visual grounding tasks, Le Chonk surpasses some frontier closed models.

Mistral's move is part of a longer narrative: the French lab has been on a tear since raising $3.3 billion in September, 20-folding revenue year-over-year and establishing itself as a credible alternative to US and Chinese labs, especially for organizations prioritizing sovereignty and control.

item.title: Mistral says "Le Chonk" can challenge the best AI models
item.description:
French company Mistral claims its new Le Chonk model rivals the best from the US and China, optimizing for coding and cyberdefense instead of competing on generalist benchmarks.

Mistral released Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter open-weight model designed to compete with the best proprietary models while remaining freely available and customizable. Le Chonk is optimized for coding, cyberdefense, manufacturing, finance, and electrical engineering—niches where Mistral's leadership says larger labs don't focus. Cofounder Guillaume Lample told WIRED that the strategy targets domains where competitors have limited interest.

The company claims Le Chonk is the most capable open-weight model built outside China and "very, very close" to some proprietary systems. Unlike Chinese labs accused of distilling smaller models from larger ones to close performance gaps, Mistral says it trained from scratch. The model costs only what compute consumes to run, a massive advantage over proprietary APIs. Mistral's recent $3.3 billion funding round and reported 20-fold revenue growth suggest the market is buying the pitch: open-weight alternatives are now viable for enterprise.

item.title: Microsoft event debuts new AI-friendly hardware and Windows changes
item.description:
Microsoft announced RTX Spark hardware, the Surface Laptop Ultra at $2,599, and Windows 11 updates designed from the ground up for local AI agents.

At its first live event in two years, Microsoft showcased a hardware and software push around local AI agents on Windows. The Surface Laptop Ultra, powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark, starts at $2,599 with unified memory allocations that let it handle both AI workloads and traditional tasks (even AAA gaming) without dedicated VRAM limits. The Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a $5,999 developer box, delivers one petaflop of AI compute.

Windows 11 is gaining Hybrid Intelligence features that let Copilot access local files and take OS-level actions. Microsoft positioned these changes as foundational: personal computing is moving toward agents running persistently in the OS, not as applications. The presentation emphasized security and governance, framing the desktop as a hardened environment for agent execution.

item.title: Google launches Developer Knowledge API, giving AI agents direct access to official documentation
item.description:
Google released a programmatic, machine-readable API for developer documentation, replacing web-scraping with structured retrieval and grounded Q&A.

Google announced the Developer Knowledge API ecosystem, an official source of truth for documentation about Google Cloud, Firebase, Android, and more. The API targets AI agents, IDE extensions, and automated workflows, replacing brittle web-scraping and stale LLM training cutoffs. The system offers semantic search, keyword search, intelligent chunking, and grounded Q&A, keeping agents accurate and token-efficient.

Frequent indexing ensures fresh documentation and minimal lag. The system comes with a gcloud CLI surface (pre-installed in Cloud Shell), client libraries for multiple languages, and an API Explorer. Developers and agents can discover, retrieve, and synthesize answers grounded in official Google docs from terminals, IDEs, and codebases. For teams building on Google Cloud, this removes a major source of hallucinations and outdated information.

item.title: Next.js 16.4 makes Cache Components the default, simplifying server-rendered personalization
item.description:
The framework defaults to Cache Components in new projects, enabling personalized pages fast and instant client navigation without the developer pain of older cache models.

Vercel released Next.js 16.4, moving Cache Components—a new programming model designed to address App Router's limitations—to the default for new projects. Cache Components bring fast initial loads, server-rendered instant client navigation, and composable, opt-in caching. Starting now, all new apps created with create-next-app have Cache Components enabled by default.

For existing apps, Next.js 16.4 ships agent-assisted upgrade tooling: `next upgrade --agent` gives agents version-specific guidance for migrating code, with dedicated Skills to automate refactorings. The release also includes memory and disk optimizations for dev, faster compile times, smaller production bundles, and React 19.3 support. Developers can opt in to Cache Components at their own pace, with tooling to ease the migration path.

item.title: Microsoft Research releases Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight reinforcement learning framework for agentic workflows
item.description:
Agent Lightning is a 3,500-line RL framework that trains agents directly in the harness used for deployment, removing the need to reimplement agent logic for training.

Microsoft Research Asia published Agent Lightning v1.0, an open-source reinforcement learning framework for training AI agents. The core innovation: agents train directly within the same harness used for deployment, eliminating the expensive reimplementation step that usually plagues agentic RL. The framework is roughly 3,500 lines of code, small enough to understand, modify, and extend.

Agent Lightning runs agents as standard Kubernetes jobs across any infrastructure—on-premises, cloud, or local—without relying on vendor-provided sandbox services. A sample training approach showed 14.6 percentage points of improvement on SWE-bench Verified using only 6,000 training samples on a small 9B-parameter model. The framework enables concrete, reproducible agent training pipelines that teams can own and modify.

item.title: Survey: AI-generated code increases debugging burden and creates comprehension gaps in teams
item.description:
A new survey finds that while AI accelerates code generation, teams spend more time debugging, and engineers lose the inherent understanding they once had from writing code themselves.

An independent survey of 300 senior engineering leaders found that AI coding agents have shifted the primary bottleneck from generation to debugging and maintenance. Teams now spend an average of 9.8 hours per week generating code but 16.9 hours per week debugging, accounting for 42% of the working week. The gap widens in mission-critical codebases where code "must be understood."

Key findings: 35% of AI-generated code reaches production before teams fully understand it. 80% of respondents said agents struggle to solve difficult problems in complex codebases. 81% experienced production incidents in the past six months. 93% reported incorrect root-cause diagnoses due to hallucination. The survey points to a structural problem: agents accelerate creation faster than teams can comprehend it, creating blind spots in debugging and maintenance.

item.title: Open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Adobe Photoshop in pure Rust
item.description:
A developer used AI to build open-source clones of Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, and other tools in Rust, vowing rapid feature parity and browser compatibility.

A software developer released Artcraft, a suite of open-source applications that replicate the interface and functionality of Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Built entirely in Rust with WebAssembly versions for browser use, the tools are clean-room implementations (designed from first principles, not copied code). Claude Opus 5.5 accelerated the reverse engineering and implementation process.

The project is in super-early alpha, with significant shortcomings acknowledged. The developer promised initial rapid progress (quickly amended from 100% parity in a month to "99% in months, not years"). For the open-source community and small teams priced out of Creative Suite, the project signals that AI-accelerated reimplementation of expensive interfaces is now plausible.

item.title: Cloudflare uses AI to probe and harden its Web Application Firewall
item.description:
Cloudflare deployed frontier AI models inside a controlled harness to probe its WAF, generating attack variations to uncover new evasion techniques and strengthen defenses.

Cloudflare placed frontier AI models inside a testing harness to probe its Web Application Firewall for vulnerabilities. The system started with attack payloads the WAF had already blocked, then used models to generate variations in encoding, placement, and delivery. Models had no access to Cloudflare's WAF rules, source code, or internal signals—effectively black-box testing. A Python harness maintained state, enforced limits, and collected responses.

Across 45 scenarios, the system generated 1,107 attempts, producing 49 findings after human review. The exercise contributed three changes to Cloudflare's Managed Ruleset. The approach demonstrates how AI can accelerate security testing while keeping humans in the verification loop.

item.title: GitHub: Secret protection must scale with software
item.description:
GitHub released a fine-tuned classifier to catch unstructured secrets, doubling detection coverage as one in three PRs now involve AI agents.

GitHub analyzed nine quarters of push data to understand how secret exposure scales with code velocity. One in three PRs now includes an AI agent; a year back, it was under 10%. Exposed credentials surface in public code roughly every two seconds, and the count doubles yearly. But GitHub's dataset challenges the "careless developer" narrative: developers' override rate (rejecting a secret protection warning) dropped from 6.6% to 3.9%, showing rising security discipline despite higher velocity.

The real challenge is volume. GitHub doubled the secret detection rate by building a fine-tuned classifier with Microsoft Applied Sciences that screens push candidates in under two milliseconds, doubling coverage of unstructured secrets. The company argues that protection must keep pace with acceleration: as agents and developers move faster, automated defenses need to intercept exposures before they reach public visibility.

item.title: Shipping JPEG XL in Chrome: a Rust decoder for memory safety
item.description:
Chrome 155 adds JPEG XL decoding via Rust, replacing C++ with a memory-safe implementation to block entire categories of image-decoder exploits.

Chrome 155 shipped JPEG XL decode support using a Rust-based decoder instead of C++. JPEG XL compresses 30-50% better than JPEG, supports lossless and HDR modes, and can transcode existing JPEG files without quality loss. Decoders sit in the renderer and parse untrusted network bytes—making them high-impact security targets.

Google built jxl-rs to prevent memory bugs entirely: no out-of-bounds reads, no heap corruption, no use-after-free flaws—eliminated at compile time. Rather than stack defense-in-depth on top of unsafe code, this approach attacks the root. SIMD optimizations (via Rust's stabilized target_feature) keep throughput on par with C++ baselines.

item.title: Atlassian and OpenAI expand partnership to turn enterprise knowledge into action
item.description:
Atlassian and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership designed to integrate frontier models with enterprise knowledge, helping teams plan, build, and deliver work.

Atlassian and OpenAI deepened their partnership to weave frontier models into Atlassian's product suite. The collaboration aims to tap enterprise data—stored in Jira, Confluence, and other Atlassian tools—and surface it to AI models for better coordination and decision support. The move signals how legacy enterprise software vendors are positioning themselves to benefit from AI adoption in large organizations.

item.title: Claude's cyber safeguards are getting more flexible — but not for everyone
item.description:
Anthropic expanded its Cyber Verification Program, breaking access into three tiers, but the restricted tier still blocks Claude Opus 5.5 in 46 out of 50 offensive-security benchmarks.

Anthropic split its Cyber Verification Program into three tiers aligned with use case. Project Glasswing (previously unrestricted for vetted security teams) moved to the lowest-restriction tier. Anthropic marketed this as expanding access, but the reality is tighter: the Defense Access tier—where most defensive security teams will land—saw Claude Opus 5.5 blocked in 46 out of 50 offensive-security benchmark runs.

The tiers match capability to scope: defensive work gets one access level; broader security work gets another. But the reality is that many teams conducting defensive work still can't access the capabilities they need.

item.title: OpenAI's Decisions API is now available in public beta
item.description:
OpenAI's Decisions API lets applications make fast structured decisions (predicates, choices, scores) at 10x speed compared to reasoning models, starting at $0.10 per million input tokens.

OpenAI released the Decisions API to public beta, a new interface for making fast structured decisions. Powered by GPT-6 Luna, the API accepts text and image inputs and outputs three types of results: predicates (probability estimates), choices (selection with confidence scores), and scores (numeric range evaluations). The company claims 10x speed improvement over reasoning models for decision tasks.

Pricing is lean: $0.10 per million input tokens with no charges for cache reads, cache writes, or output tokens. Early users reported mixed results compared to TypeSafe's Jev decision model: Decisions API matches Jev on narrow yes/no checks but lags on nuanced judgment calls. Speed is slightly slower on Jev's typical response.

item.title: Decision models are suddenly everywhere
item.description:
OpenAI, Perplexity, Cloudflare, and Amazon all released decision models this month, signaling a new category where speed and cost matter more than reasoning.

Decision models are rapidly becoming a standard AI primitive. Multiple labs released versions this month: OpenAI, Perplexity, Cloudflare, and Amazon all launched decision models. OpenAI's runs on GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 per million input tokens (input-only pricing). Competitors chose open-weight models that developers can download and run in-house.

The category differs fundamentally from reasoning models: decisions are narrow, structured outputs where latency and cost matter more than deep reasoning. Applications include video game pathfinding, real-time routing, and content classification. OpenAI demonstrated combining Decisions API with computer-use capabilities for real-time visual decision-making (e.g., analyzing camera frames to direct a robot).

item.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
item.description:
Microsoft's "Hybrid Intelligence" lets Copilot access local files and take OS-level actions, turning the assistant from a chat interface into a cross-app orchestrator.

Microsoft unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, an upgrade to Copilot that grants file system access on your PC and cross-application orchestration capabilities. In a demo, the company showed Copilot handling a tax filing request: it found relevant documents across folders, renamed them, packaged them, and composed a draft email—all unguided. The system blends local and cloud AI to balance privacy, latency, and capability.

Hybrid Intelligence features will roll out over the next couple months. The company also announced a new Windows search experience with quick actions from the search bar. The search experience arrives this fall.

item.title: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed
item.description:
ThinkingBox benchmark finds that 67% of agent failures leave no trace in tool calls or responses—the agent sounds correct while leaving the wrong database state.

Microsoft and Hugging Face published ThinkingBox, a benchmark that grades AI agents on terminal backend state and side effects, not just tool calls and responses. The researchers ran 507 stateful business workflows 20 times each against various models and found a critical gap: 67% of failed runs ended without a tool error. The agent sounded correct; it was the database that disagreed.

Example: an agent handling a warranty claim made nine well-formed tool calls, correctly followed refund policy, and closed the ticket—all while missing a critical detail (the carrier exception was still open). Only the database state reveals the failure. This gap is what ThinkingBox measures and why most agent benchmarks miss real failures.

item.title: Nous Research confirms $1.5B valuation, launches Hermes agents for business
item.description:
Nous Research raised $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation, deploying Hermes agents (open-source model cloned 24 million times) into enterprise workflows.

Nous Research closed a $90 million Series B at $1.5 billion valuation, with backing from Robot Ventures, Nvidia, Union Square Ventures, Menlo Ventures, Samsung, and 1789 Capital. The three-year-old startup, known for the open-source Hermes Agent, is expanding into enterprise with "Hermes for Businesses," allowing companies to deploy customized AI agents for multi-step workflows. Hermes Agent has been cloned over 24 million times and reportedly drives roughly 2.5% of global AI token usage.

Nous was at $36 million annualized revenue by mid-September and expects to top $100 million before year's end. The funding accelerates its pivot from open-source developer tools to enterprise-grade agentic platforms.

item.title: Robot data startup Mecka AI nabs $60M from Sequoia
item.description:
Mecka AI raised a $60 million Series B from Sequoia to scale its human motion-capture operation, training humanoid robots with real-world data.

Mecka AI closed a $60 million Series B at $500 million valuation, led by Sequoia. The company's business model: pay people to perform everyday tasks (coffee-making, auto repair) while wearing motion sensors and holding smartphones, then use that footage to train robot models. Launched in 2024, Mecka mirrors what Scale AI and other data-labeling vendors did for LLMs: becoming the pipeline that feeds human-created training examples to AI systems.

Other robotics data startups like XDOF are in similar fundraising rounds. Larger data platforms like Scale AI are also expanding into robotics. The activity signals that the bottleneck for humanoid robots is shifting from architecture to training data quality.

item.title: Meta and Microsoft take steps to reduce employee usage of Claude AI
item.description:
Meta and Microsoft are reducing internal employee access to Claude, signaling competitive tension between OpenAI and Anthropic in enterprise adoption.

Meta and Microsoft each implemented internal restrictions on Claude access, blocking their own staff from using Anthropic's models. The actions betray genuine competition: large labs don't restrict models they see as irrelevant. When you lock your own engineers out, it's a public signal that you view the competitor as a real threat.

item.title: Spanner Omni Reaches GA, replacing Google's atomic clocks and file system with software
item.description:
Google released Spanner Omni to general availability, a version of its distributed SQL database that runs anywhere—your racks, other clouds, or a laptop—using software to replace hardware dependencies.

Google announced general availability of Spanner Omni, enabling its distributed SQL database to run on customer-controlled infrastructure. The challenge: Spanner's original design relied on Colossus (Google's proprietary file system) and TrueTime (a clock service with atomic clocks and GPS). Spanner Omni substitutes software equivalents that achieve similar results.

The file layer is a Colossus-like abstraction layered over attached local storage, replicating data across nodes and handling resharding automatically. Time synchronization is solved through software algorithms; Spanner tolerates weaker clock guarantees than TrueTime provides. The operational reality, though, shifts: your infrastructure becomes your failure domain. Patching, upgrades, and failure recovery become your team's responsibility, not Google's.
